title: Colorado judge holds ICE officials in contempt over re-arrests
h1: A federal judge in Colorado found ICE officials in contempt for re-arresting immigrants moments after courts ordered them freed
description: Judge Charlotte Sweeney ruled Nov. 18, 2026, that Colorado ICE officials were in contempt over quick re-arrests but set no sanctions since the practice ended.
standfirst: U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney found that top Colorado immigration officials defied release orders by detaining people again within minutes. She declined to punish them because ICE has stopped, but warned she could reopen the matter.
keywords: ICE contempt Colorado, Judge Charlotte Sweeney ICE ruling, ICE re-arrest after release Colorado, Ramon Quintero Alvarez habeas, Nathan Rasper ICE Denver
takeaways: Judge Charlotte Sweeney issued a 15-page contempt ruling on Wednesday, Nov. 18, 2026.
At least 18 people in Colorado were held too long or re-arrested soon after ordered releases over about six weeks, according to the reporting.
No fines or other sanctions were imposed because ICE ended the practice, but the judge said new violations could reopen the case.
body: A federal judge in Colorado has found top Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Homeland Security officials in contempt of court for detaining immigrants again almost as soon as judges ordered them released. U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney issued the 15-page ruling on Wednesday, Nov. 18, according to Colorado Public Radio reporting published by The Colorado Sun. In it, she wrote that the re-detention policy "made a mockery of court orders."

The case centered on Ramon Quintero Alvarez, a Wyoming resident born in Mexico who had petitioned for release from the immigration detention center in Aurora. When the U.S. Attorney's Office did not respond to the petition, his release was triggered, and ICE took him back into custody shortly after he walked out, Colorado Politics reported from a Nov. 9 hearing.

At that hearing, assistant field office director Nichole Black testified that she was told to re-detain people released through habeas petitions if they had some kind of criminal history. Nathan Rasper, the acting head of ICE's Denver field office, said he gave that verbal instruction, believed the agency could lawfully re-arrest people after correcting paperwork, and had since stopped the practice.

The Sun's report says at least 18 people in Colorado were held longer than allowed or re-arrested within minutes of a court-ordered release over roughly six weeks. Immigration lawyers believe the real number is higher because some detainees have no attorney.

Judges can fine officials or order conduct to stop, but Sweeney concluded that ending the practice had cured the contempt and declined further action. She warned that any new violations could lead her to reopen the matter. U.S. Attorney Peter McNeilly declined to comment on the order, according to the report.

Other federal judges in Colorado have issued their own limits. Colorado Politics reported that Judge Gordon Gallagher and Judge Philip Brimmer each entered orders in early November restricting re-arrests of people they had ordered freed.
